passage:
I'm Dhruv. Last year someone I'd been talking to online for two months, "Maya", asked me to buy gift cards worth fifteen thousand. Her mother was in hospital; she'd pay me back Friday.
I liked Maya a lot. I still felt the tug. But after reading about scams, I had made myself one rule: if someone I've never met asks for money in any form, gift cards, crypto, a transfer, that's a stop sign. Not a maybe. A stop.
So I stopped. I didn't argue with her. I called Chaitanya, who has known me since school, and read him the messages. He didn't laugh. He said, "Good that you called. Let's report it."
We reported the profile to the app, and I filed a complaint on the cybercrime portal. It took twenty minutes.
The embarrassing part was admitting I'd fallen for the chat at all. Chaitanya said the people who run these scams do it for a living. That helped.

qa.q: What did Maya ask Dhruv to buy?
qa.a: Maya asked Dhruv to buy gift cards worth fifteen thousand.

qa.q: What did Dhruv feel when the request came?
qa.a: Dhruv still felt a tug of affection for Maya, but the rule made the request feel like a clear stop sign.

qa.q: Which of Dhruv's choices worked, and why?
qa.a: Treating the request as a stop sign, calling Chaitanya instead of arguing with Maya, and reporting to the app and the cybercrime portal protected the money and possibly others.

qa.q: How does Chaitanya see Dhruv's embarrassment?
qa.a: Chaitanya sees it without blame, reminding Dhruv that scammers do this for a living, so falling for the chat is not foolish.

grounding: A person treats an online contact's request for gift cards as a stop sign, tells Chaitanya and reports it, and is supported rather than blamed.

Supervisor's note, 3 March. Vaibhav, accounts team.
Pallavi asked to speak privately after the morning huddle. She showed me messages from a man she met on a matrimonial site, "Dr Karan", who says he works on an oil rig. After six weeks of daily calls, audio only, he asked her to pay a customs fee for a gift parcel he had sent.
She told me she knew at once it was a stop sign, because he had asked for money and they had never met. She had not paid. She said she felt foolish for having liked him.
I told her she had done exactly the right thing, and that these schemes are run by professionals; liking someone is not foolish.
Actions today: sat with her while she reported the profile to the site and filed a complaint on the cybercrime portal. Gave her the afternoon off. Will check on her Thursday.

qa.a: She felt foolish for having liked him, even though she had spotted the scam.

qa.a: Vaibhav told her she had done the right thing, reminded her these schemes are run by professionals, and sat with her while she reported the profile and filed a complaint.

Wednesday night
Today "Aarush" asked me for gift cards. He said his work account was blocked in Oman and he needed ₹15,000 in gift card codes to pay a fine, just until Friday.
We've been talking for two months. He's funny and gentle. For a second, I reached for my wallet.
Then I remembered the talk at our office on scams. Any request for cash, vouchers or digital coins from someone you've never met is a stop sign. Always.
So I stopped. I told him, "I don't send money to anyone I haven't met in person." He sent five angry messages.
I called Zainab. She came over with samosas and sat with me while I reported his profile on the app and filed a complaint on the cyber police portal.
I feel sad, like something I liked has died. But Zainab said, "You did everything right." I'm Nirmala, and I'm proud of myself tonight.

qa.a: Gift cards: ₹15,000 in gift card codes.

qa.a: Zainab is supportive, bringing samosas and saying Nirmala did everything right, without any blame.

In the kasba where Lokesh ran his mobile repair shop, everyone knew he was "engaged" to a woman from Mumbai he'd met online. For weeks he'd smiled at his phone behind the counter.
On Thursday she messaged: her visa for a job in Canada was stuck and she needed ₹60,000 by Monday, or she'd lose it. "I'll pay you back when we marry."
Lokesh stared at the message. He had never met her. The video calls always "dropped."
That evening he closed the shop early and went to his sister Tanuja's house. He showed her everything. His voice shook. "Am I a fool, didi?"
"No," Tanuja said. "You're a kind man someone is trying to use." She made him tea.
The next morning, they took the bus together to the cyber police station at the district headquarters. The officer took the screenshots and said, "Good that you didn't pay. Many people come after."

qa.q: How much did the woman say she needed by Monday?
qa.a: ₹60,000 by Monday.

qa.q: How did Lokesh feel when he showed Tanuja the messages?
qa.a: Lokesh felt ashamed and shaken, his voice trembling as he asked if he was a fool.

qa.q: What steps did Lokesh take after the request?
qa.a: He didn't pay, told his sister Tanuja, and went with her to the cyber police station the next morning.

qa.q: How did Tanuja respond to her brother?
qa.a: Tanuja responded with kindness and no blame, calling him a kind man someone was trying to use.

grounding: It shows an adult treating an online fiancée's money request as a stop sign, telling his sister and reporting it to cyber police.

passage: Selin was halfway through her shift at the bakery in Berlin when the message came: "Babe, my visa is stuck. I need gift cards today or I can't fly to you." For six weeks Daniel had been the best part of her evenings. Her stomach dropped, but her mind went to a line her sister often repeated: if someone you've never met asks for money, stop. She didn't reply. At break she showed Tuan, who worked the counter with her. He read it twice. "Gift cards for a visa? That's not how visas work." He didn't laugh or ask how she could fall for it. He just pulled up a chair. Together they took screenshots, reported the profile on the app, and filed an online report with the police. Selin felt sad and hollow, and a little foolish. Tuan bought her a pretzel. "You caught it before it cost you anything. That's the part that counts."

qa.q: What did Daniel say he needed the gift cards for?
qa.a: He said his visa was stuck and he couldn't fly to Selin without them.

qa.q: How did Selin feel after reporting it?
qa.a: Selin felt sad and hollow, and a little foolish, even though she had stopped in time.

qa.a: She treated the money request as a stop sign, didn't reply, told a coworker, and reported the profile to the app and to the police.

qa.a: Tuan took it seriously without blame or mockery and helped report it, which makes it easier for Selin to seek help instead of hiding in shame.
